executive_summary: JFrog provides two complementary paths for giving AI coding agents safe, governed access to artifact context: (1) JFrog Skills — open-source AI agent skills (jfrog/jfrog-skills on GitHub) that let agents search artifacts, check CVEs, verify curation, trace builds, and manage storage via natural language, using a three-tier tool selection strategy (MCP → jf CLI → REST/GraphQL); and (2) the JFrog MCP Server — a remote SaaS MCP server (beta) that provides structured JFrog platform access to MCP clients like VS Code, Cursor, Claude, Kiro, and Codex via OAuth authentication. The Cursor plugin bundles both: it vendors the jfrog-skills and adds an Agent Guard feature for discovering, installing, configuring, and removing MCP servers from the JFrog AI Catalog. The key editorial angle is that JFrog treats 'agent skills as the new packages' — the same supply chain governance (curation, vulnerability scanning, provenance) that JFrog applies to software packages now applies to AI agent capabilities. The winning article should be a practical guide covering both integration paths, comparing when to use Skills vs the MCP Server, with setup steps, security considerations, and a decision framework.
new_findings_from_2026_07_04: The JFrog Skills ARCHITECTURE.md reveals a sophisticated progressive disclosure model: the agent reads only SKILL.md + 1-3 reference files per operation, keeping context focused.

The three-tier tool selection strategy is: JFrog MCP tools (Tier 1, preferred, no env check needed) → jf CLI commands (Tier 2) → jf api REST/GraphQL (Tier 3, last resort). Binary artifact operations (download/upload) always use native CLI commands.
The base jfrog skill has 8 domain model reference files, 4 operations files, 3 OneModel GraphQL files, 2 API gap files, and 7 infrastructure/pattern files — all organized for progressive disclosure.

The skill cache at ~/.jfrog/skills-cache/ is restricted to only two artifacts: jfrog-skill-state.json (env check output) and onemodel-schema-<server-id>.graphql. All other scratch data must go to /tmp.
The environment check script (check-environment.sh) outputs a user-agent string following RFC 7231 format: jfrog-skills/<v> [(tool=<harness>; model=<slug>; ...)] jfrog-cli-go/<v>.

The JFrog MCP Server Tools page lists extensive toolsets across: Access (Tokens, OIDC, Projects, Roles, Stages, Users/Groups), Artifactory (Repositories, Packages, Builds, Federation, Storage), Security, Curation, Distribution, Evidence, AppTrust, and Workers.

The jf api endpoint uses product-prefix routing: /artifactory/api/..., /xray/api/..., /access/api/..., /evidence/api/..., /apptrust/api/..., /distribution/api/..., /lifecycle/api/..., /onemodel/api/v1/graphql — all auto-authenticated via the active jf config server.

key_facts.fact: JFrog Skills (jfrog/jfrog-skills) is an open-source repository (Apache 2.0, beta) with three skills: jfrog (base), jfrog-package-safety-and-download, and jfrog-ai-catalog-skills.

JFrog Skills use a three-tier tool selection strategy: JFrog MCP tools (preferred, Tier 1) → jf CLI commands (fallback, Tier 2) → jf api REST/GraphQL (last resort, Tier 3). Binary artifact operations (download/upload) always use native CLI commands regardless of tier.

The base jfrog skill covers CLI setup, artifact operations (search, download, version queries, metadata), security queries (CVE lookups, upgrade safety, exposure findings), AQL queries, and GraphQL (OneModel).
The jfrog-package-safety-and-download skill checks whether npm, Maven, PyPI, Go, and other packages are safe, curated, or allowed before downloading through Artifactory.
The jfrog-ai-catalog-skills skill lets agents discover, install, update, and publish agent skills in the JFrog AI Catalog.
JFrog Skills require jf CLI ≥ 2.100.0, curl, and jq on PATH, plus a configured JFrog instance (jf config add).
Installation: npx skills add git@github.com:jfrog/jfrog-skills.git -g --skill jfrog --skill jfrog-package-safety-and-download --skill jfrog-ai-catalog-skills

The JFrog MCP Server (official, remote/SaaS) is in beta, available to JFrog Cloud subscribers. It provides tools for repository management, artifact search, catalog/curation, and security monitoring via OAuth authentication.

The official JFrog MCP Server requires no installation — it is maintained on JFrog SaaS. Admin enables it on a JPD, then users add the URL (https://<JFROG_PLATFORM_URL>/mcp) to their MCP client config.

There is also an experimental community MCP server (jfrog/mcp-jfrog) with 119 stars, self-hosted via npm or Docker, with 22+ tools including repository CRUD, AQL queries, build tracking, runtime monitoring, and Xray scanning.

The JFrog Cursor Plugin (v0.5.0+) uses the official jfrog-skills v0.11.0 and adds Agent Guard — a feature to discover, install, configure, update, and remove MCP servers from the JFrog AI Catalog approved for a project.

Agent Guard handles MCP server secrets securely: the agent cannot set sensitive values directly; it returns a CLI command for the user to run in their terminal, keeping API keys and tokens out of chat history.

JFrog positions 'Agent Skills are the New Packages of AI' — applying the same supply chain governance (curation, vulnerability scanning, provenance) to AI agent capabilities that it applies to software packages.
The JFrog AI Catalog is a central registry for governing agent skills and MCP servers per project, with approval workflows, version management, and policy enforcement.

recommended_angle.headline: JFrog Skills and MCP Tools Guide 2026: Give Your Coding Agents Safe Artifact Context
recommended_angle.dek: JFrog Skills and the JFrog MCP Server give AI coding agents governed access to artifacts, vulnerabilities, and curation data. Here is how both work, when to use each, and how to set them up safely.
recommended_angle.differentiator: This is the first guide that covers both JFrog Skills (open-source agent skills) and the JFrog MCP Server (remote SaaS) as complementary paths, with a decision framework, setup steps for each, security considerations, and the 'agent skills as packages' supply chain governance angle.
recommended_angle.point_of_view: JFrog is uniquely positioned to govern AI agent capabilities the same way it governs software packages — through curation, vulnerability scanning, and provenance tracking. Skills and MCP tools are two sides of the same coin: Skills give agents natural-language access to JFrog data, while the MCP Server provides structured tool access. Both need the same supply chain governance.

recommended_outline.h2: Why JFrog for AI Coding Agents?
points: The problem: coding agents need artifact context (versions, vulnerabilities, licenses) but direct access to Artifactory is risky.
JFrog's thesis: 'Agent Skills are the New Packages of AI' — apply the same governance.

Open-source AI agent skills (jfrog/jfrog-skills, Apache 2.0, beta).
Three skills: jfrog (base), jfrog-package-safety-and-download, jfrog-ai-catalog-skills.
Three-tier tool selection: MCP → jf CLI → jf api (REST/GraphQL).

Installable via npx skills add in any AI coding agent (Cursor, Claude Code, etc.).

recommended_outline.h2: What can you do with JFrog Skills?
points: Search and download artifacts by name, version, SHA256, path, or AQL query.
Check CVEs, upgrade safety, security profiles, exposure findings (secrets, IaC, AppSec).

Trace builds: artifacts, dependencies, VCS info, checksum verification.
Manage storage: find stale/large/undownloaded artifacts, property queries.
Administer platform: CLI setup, multi-instance management, access tokens.
Discover and install AI Catalog skills.
Execute multi-step workflows (e.g., 'upgrade X to latest safe version').

recommended_outline.h2: What is the JFrog MCP Server?
points: Official remote MCP Server (SaaS, beta) — no installation needed.
OAuth authentication — no API keys to manage.
Tools: repository CRUD, AQL search, package info/versions/vulnerabilities, curation status, Xray summaries.

recommended_outline.h2: JFrog Skills vs JFrog MCP Server: which to use?
points: Skills: richer capabilities (build tracing, storage management, multi-step workflows), open-source, works in any agent that supports npx skills.
MCP Server: zero-install, OAuth-secured, structured tool interface, SaaS-managed.
Use Skills when you need deep JFrog platform operations and multi-step workflows.
Use MCP Server when you want a lightweight, managed connection for basic artifact queries.
Both can coexist — Skills can fall back to MCP tools when available.

faq_targets.question: What are JFrog Skills?
faq_targets.answer: JFrog Skills are open-source AI agent skills (jfrog/jfrog-skills on GitHub) that let coding agents interact with the JFrog Platform through natural language — searching artifacts, checking vulnerabilities, verifying curation, tracing builds, and managing storage.

faq_targets.question: What is the JFrog MCP Server?
faq_targets.answer: The JFrog MCP Server is a remote SaaS MCP server (beta) that provides structured JFrog Platform access to MCP clients like VS Code, Cursor, Claude, and Codex via OAuth authentication, with no installation required.

faq_targets.question: How do JFrog Skills differ from the JFrog MCP Server?
faq_targets.answer: JFrog Skills are open-source agent skills installed via npx skills add, offering deeper platform operations and multi-step workflows. The JFrog MCP Server is a managed SaaS service with OAuth auth, offering structured tool access for basic artifact queries.

faq_targets.question: Can I use both JFrog Skills and the MCP Server together?
faq_targets.answer: Yes. JFrog Skills use a three-tier tool selection strategy where MCP tools are the preferred tier. When a JFrog MCP tool exists and succeeds, the skill uses it; otherwise it falls back to CLI or API.

faq_targets.question: What is JFrog Agent Guard?
faq_targets.answer: Agent Guard is a feature in the JFrog Cursor Plugin that lets you discover, install, configure, update, and remove MCP servers from the JFrog AI Catalog through natural language, with secrets handled via CLI commands rather than chat.

faq_targets.question: Do I need a JFrog Cloud subscription to use the MCP Server?
faq_targets.answer: Yes. The official JFrog MCP Server is available to JFrog Cloud (SaaS) subscribers. An admin must enable it on a JPD. The experimental community MCP server (jfrog/mcp-jfrog) can be self-hosted with any JFrog instance.

faq_targets.question: Is JFrog Skills production-ready?
faq_targets.answer: JFrog Skills are in beta under the Apache 2.0 license. The repository states behavior, APIs, and structure may change without notice during the 0.x release cycle, and JFrog makes no guarantees of backward compatibility.

writer_notes: Distinguish clearly between the three JFrog MCP offerings: (1) official remote MCP Server (SaaS, beta), (2) experimental community MCP server (jfrog/mcp-jfrog, self-hosted), and (3) MCP tools referenced in the Skills architecture as Tier 1.
The 'JFrog Skills' and 'JFrog MCP Server' are complementary, not competing — Skills can use MCP tools when available.
Emphasize the supply chain governance angle: JFrog applies the same curation, vulnerability scanning, and provenance to agent skills that it applies to software packages.
Avoid claiming the experimental MCP server is production-ready — the README explicitly says it is not officially supported.
The Cursor Plugin is the most complete integration — it bundles Skills + Agent Guard for MCP management.
Include concrete prompt examples grouped by developer role (frontend, backend, security, platform).
